topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health contexts; competency frameworks may require adaptation for Australian health system structures, funding models, and regulatory environments.
takeaways: Identify which digital health competencies are most critical for your workforce by reviewing the framework's structured competency domains rather than assuming all digital skills are equally important.

Use the European competency framework as a benchmarking tool to audit gaps in your team's current capabilities, but validate recommendations against Australian public health priorities and NHMRC guidelines.

Consider piloting competency assessment and upskilling pathways using this framework's structure, but adapt content to reflect Australian health policy, technology infrastructure, and regulatory requirements (e.g., privacy legislation, accreditation standards).

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on dental education curriculum design. Competency framework may not transfer directly to other professional disciplines or general workforce AI literacy programmes, though the methodological approach could be adapted.
takeaways: Develop role-specific AI competency frameworks aligned with professional practice requirements rather than generic AI skills — this dental education model shows how to map AI capabilities to actual job tasks and patient outcomes.

Structure competency development across multiple levels (foundational, intermediate, advanced) to accommodate learners with varying prior experience and allow progressive skill-building over a programme.

Include both technical understanding and ethical/critical thinking dimensions — competency frameworks should address how professionals make decisions about when and how to use AI, not just technical operation.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity without full article access — appears to be a broad educational analysis, but geographic scope and sector coverage are unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Generation Z requires proactive educational intervention in AI literacy; organisations should consider partnering with educational institutions to embed AI skills training into curricula before hiring.
Innovative delivery methods for AI education are critical — explore blended learning approaches (online + practical) that suit younger cohorts' preferences and learning styles.
Start early with foundational AI concepts rather than waiting for employees to arrive with gaps — preventative education reduces downstream upskilling burden on organisations.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to middle school education context; geographic scope unclear from title and snippet. Findings may not generalise directly to adult workplace AI literacy development or other educational levels.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation — consider how AI skills connect to existing digital, information, and data literacy capabilities in your training programs.

A holistic approach to AI literacy for middle school suggests starting foundational AI concepts early and integrating them across subjects, which could inform how organisations scaffold AI literacy for diverse employee populations with varying prior knowledge.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely focused on US public health education context; generalisability to Australian health faculties would depend on details not evident from title/snippet alone. Public health sector specificity may limit application to other disciplines.
takeaways: Faculty development programs are critical for shifting educator mindsets from AI resistance to readiness — without this foundation, institutional AI literacy initiatives will struggle regardless of student-facing curriculum design.

Targeted professional development for teaching staff should address not just technical AI knowledge but also the psychological barriers and concerns that fuel resistance to change in educational settings.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity from snippet alone, but likely focuses on higher education sector globally. Applicability to workplace AI development in non-academic settings may require assessment of specific strategies discussed.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your workforce by examining frameworks developed in higher education contexts — these may differ from technical versus foundational literacy needs in your organisation.

Consider structured pedagogical approaches (curriculum design, scaffolded learning, assessment methods) from higher education that could be adapted to employee upskilling programmes rather than adopting ad-hoc training.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — would depend on sample size, industry sectors, and geographic scope, which are not detailed here. Frontiers articles typically draw from diverse international submissions, but specific limitations cannot be assessed without full text.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in your team as a precondition for them to leverage AI tools as genuine job resources rather than threats — employees with stronger PsyCap are more likely to experiment with AI and drive innovation.

When introducing AI systems, frame them explicitly as tools that augment human capability and decision-making, then invest in confidence-building and problem-solving skills development so employees feel equipped to use them effectively.

Monitor whether AI adoption is increasing or decreasing psychological capital in your workforce — if employees feel disempowered or helpless about AI decisions, innovation will stall; proactive coaching and transparent algorithmic feedback loops help maintain employee agency.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — sample location and size not evident. Findings on paternalistic leadership may have regional applicability constraints, as this leadership style varies significantly across cultures.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customising AI systems to their workflows (AI crafting), which strengthens collaboration and reduces resistance.
Leaders using a paternalistic approach can leverage care and involvement in employees' AI adoption journey to build ownership and increase willingness to work alongside AI systems.
Design AI implementation processes that allow employees agency in shaping how AI integrates into their work, rather than imposing top-down solutions.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — presents conceptual concerns and risks without empirical data or specific organisational context. Findings are illustrative rather than research-based, so applicability depends on your workplace's AI adoption patterns.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational guidelines on which AI tools employees can use for personal support (mental health, financial, legal advice) to prevent over-reliance on unvetted systems that may provide harmful recommendations.

Create awareness campaigns highlighting the risks of treating AI as a substitute for professional support — particularly for sensitive domains like mental health or medical decisions — to help employees make informed choices.

Provide access to legitimate professional support channels (EAP, counselling, HR) as alternatives to AI, and ensure managers understand the organisational policy so they can guide teams appropriately.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework applicable across sectors, but generalisability depends on the specific studies reviewed and whether they span diverse organisational contexts and geographies.
takeaways: Be aware of the Automation–Augmentation Paradox: generative AI can either replace employee knowledge work (automation) or enhance it (augmentation)—outcomes depend on how organisations design roles and training, not on the technology alone.

When implementing generative AI, intentionally structure workflows to promote knowledge augmentation rather than deskilling; employees need clear guidance on how AI tools complement their expertise rather than substitute for it.

Monitor changes in employee knowledge-sharing and learning behaviours after AI adoption; passive tool use without deliberate skill development can erode institutional knowledge and employee capability over time.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — the snippet provides no information about sample size, geography, sector, or methodology. Full article details needed to assess how broadly findings apply.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical buffer against negative mental health outcomes when introducing AI tools; organisations should assess and strengthen psychological safety practices before or alongside AI implementation.

AI adoption alone does not inevitably harm worker wellbeing — the relationship is conditional on workplace culture factors, suggesting interventions targeting psychological safety may mitigate depression risk.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geographic location, sector focus, or methodology. Full article review needed to assess whether findings apply broadly to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Building AI self-efficacy in staff may buffer against job stress and improve cybersecurity compliance behaviour — consider targeted upskilling programs that boost confidence in AI-adjacent security tools.

Job stress appears to be a mediating factor in cybersecurity behaviour; organisations should assess whether stress levels are undermining security practices and address root causes alongside technical training.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner guidance reflects consulting experience but lacks disclosed empirical validation, geographic scope, or sector specificity. Applicability may vary by organisational context and industry.
takeaways: Move beyond 'adoption' framing to 'adaptation' — design change interventions that build new behaviours and mindsets rather than simply implementing technology, focusing on how people need to work differently with AI.

Identify and target the specific human behaviours required for AI success in your context before rolling out training or tools — misalignment between required behaviours and change design is a common failure point.

Use a behaviour-change approach (e.g., habit formation, social norms, feedback loops) alongside technical implementation to embed sustainable AI-enabled ways of working across your team or organisation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified geographic scope or empirical data. Findings and recommendations likely reflect US business school context and may not directly apply to Australian employment law, industrial relations, or organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and processes in your organisation where AI adoption could disrupt workflows, then proactively communicate changes and upskilling pathways to affected teams before implementation.

Design transition support that goes beyond technical training — include psychological safety measures and career counselling to help employees see AI as a tool augmenting their work rather than replacing it.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, unable to assess sample characteristics, geographic scope, sector representation, or methodological rigor. Generalisability depends on study design and participant composition.
takeaways: Understanding whether employees actively reshape their roles in response to AI (approach behaviours) or withdraw from AI-adjacent tasks (avoidance behaviours) can help design adoption strategies that encourage constructive job crafting rather than disengagement.

Organisational leaders can use approach-avoidance framing to diagnose how employees are psychologically responding to AI tools—those showing avoidance patterns may need additional support, skill-building, or role clarity to re-engage with technology.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis likely draws on consulting engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but the specific sample, methodology, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Reframe AI adoption as fundamentally a workforce change initiative, not just a technology rollout — this requires upfront investment in identifying which roles will transform, which will be displaced, and which new capabilities are needed.
Design behaviour change interventions that address employee concerns about job security and relevance early, rather than waiting for resistance to emerge after AI implementation begins.
Plan for reskilling and role redesign in parallel with AI deployment — employees are more likely to embrace AI if they see a clear pathway to meaningful work in the post-AI environment.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to Chinese primary and secondary school contexts. Results may not generalise to other educational systems with different institutional structures, teacher autonomy levels, or cultural attitudes toward technology adoption. Limited applicability to Australian school settings without contextual adaptation.
takeaways: AI tools can paradoxically inhibit innovative teaching if teachers perceive them as threats rather than challenges—frame AI adoption messaging around opportunity and skill-building rather than job displacement to shift mindset.

Teacher efficacy and psychological safety are critical mediators: support teachers in developing AI competence through training and creating low-stakes experimentation spaces, as this determines whether they embrace or resist innovative uses.

Implementation context matters significantly—simply introducing AI tools won't drive behaviour change; pair technology rollout with clear communication about how AI augments rather than replaces teaching practice.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but specific case studies and client contexts are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may reflect practices in large organisations more than SMEs.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a standalone training programme — this positioning increases stakeholder buy-in and integration with broader business transformation efforts.

Design upskilling interventions that address both capability gaps and resistance to change; pair technical learning with change management practices (e.g. storytelling, early wins, peer champions) to shift mindsets and behaviours.
Create feedback loops and measurement mechanisms during rollout to monitor adoption barriers and adjustment fatigue, allowing you to pace change and reinforce progress with your teams.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The surprising disconnect between intense romance and a couple’s sex life - PsyPost
articles.snippet: The surprising disconnect between intense romance and a couple’s sex life  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — a brief news summary without access to underlying research methodology, sample details, or geographic scope. Findings may reflect a specific study population and cannot be assumed universally applicable.
takeaways: Romantic intensity and sexual satisfaction aren't as tightly linked as popular culture suggests — couples can feel deeply in love while having less frequent or satisfying sex, challenging the myth that 'real love' equals passionate intimacy.

The finding is counterintuitive because most relationship narratives conflate romance with sexuality, making people assume thriving emotional connection automatically translates to thriving physical connection — it apparently doesn't always work that way.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, generalisability cannot be assessed. The findings likely depend on the specific personality framework used, sample characteristics, and experimental context.
takeaways: Some personality types have strikingly better recall for surprising moments — suggesting our brains don't treat unexpected events equally, which is counterintuitive given how 'memorable' surprise feels to everyone.
This reveals why eyewitness accounts of shocking events vary wildly between people: personality shapes not just how surprised we feel, but what we actually encode into memory.
A fun reminder that the 'flashbulb memory' effect (the idea we remember shocking moments with perfect clarity) isn't universal — it's filtered through who we are as people.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline framing suggests this is a news summary of underlying research; actual scope, sample size, and methodology details are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies find structural or functional differences in people with psychopathic traits, though the snippet doesn't reveal what the difference actually is—a reminder that 'shocking' headlines often obscure the actual science.
Psychopathy exists on a spectrum and isn't monolithic; brain differences alone don't determine behaviour, making pop-science coverage of neuroscience especially prone to oversimplification.

The public finds neuroscience fascinating precisely because it feels objective, yet interpreting brain scans is surprisingly complex—this story's appeal shows how readily we're drawn to biological 'explanations' for behaviour.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-style coverage of research without visible detail on sample size, methodology, or geographic scope. The underlying study's generalisability cannot be assessed from this snippet alone.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism—typically seen as off-putting—may paradoxically attract romantic partners, challenging the intuition that narcissistic traits are universally unappealing.

The finding highlights how personality traits linked to dominance, confidence, or assertiveness can have unexpected social payoffs in attraction contexts, even when those same traits harm relationships long-term.

This research is a good reminder that 'successful' attraction and 'successful' relationships operate on different psychological principles—what works for an initial spark may undermine lasting connection.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a computational analysis of wine reviews; sample size, geographic origin of reviewers, and review platforms not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Wine preferences and review language reveal personality traits in unexpected ways — what you write about wine can say as much about you as what you drink.
AI can detect subtle personality signals in everyday writing (like wine reviews) that humans might miss, offering a fun lens on how personality shapes our everyday tastes and opinions.
The finding is surprising because wine appreciation is often treated as purely gustatory, but review text analysis suggests it's deeply tied to individual personality expression and values.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest musical preference patterns are consistent across diverse cultures and geographic regions.
takeaways: Personality traits show up in music choices regardless of where you live — suggesting fundamental links between how people are wired and what sounds appeal to them.
Despite massive cultural differences across the globe, people with similar personalities gravitate toward similar genres, revealing something universal about human psychology.
Your Spotify playlist might be a more reliable personality indicator than you'd expect, even when comparing listeners from completely different parts of the world.

topics.label: Psychological Safety

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified from snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings based on academic sector multicultural teams; applicability to non-academic organisational contexts and single-culture teams unclear. Geographic scope not specified in snippet.
takeaways: AI tools can augment inclusive leadership practices by helping leaders systematically identify and mitigate gender bias in team interactions and decision-making — test whether your organisation's existing AI systems (e.g., meeting analytics, feedback tools) could surface gendered communication patterns your team might otherwise miss.

Algorithmic support for inclusive leadership is most effective when paired with leader awareness and intent — ensure leaders understand *why* AI-assisted inclusion matters and are trained to act on its insights, rather than treating it as a passive compliance tool.

Multicultural academic teams may experience compounded exclusion (gender + cultural) that single-axis approaches overlook — assess whether your psychological safety interventions account for intersecting identities, not just gender or cultural diversity alone.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across geographies and sectors, though specific findings may vary by country and industry. Sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet, limiting assessment of representativeness.
takeaways: Identify which psychological safety concerns (e.g., job security, workplace fairness, speaking up) are most prevalent among your workforce by comparing results to your organisation's pulse survey data.

Use the global trends to benchmark your current culture against peer expectations — if employees report low psychological safety in hope/fear dimensions, this signals need for targeted trust-building interventions.
Regional and sectoral variations in the data can help tailor messaging and safety initiatives to specific employee groups rather than applying one-size-fits-all approaches.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone. Without access to the full article, the geographic scope, sample size, and sector representation cannot be assessed. Findings on depression and psychological safety related to AI adoption may vary significantly by organisational culture, country, and industry context.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediating factor in how AI adoption affects employee wellbeing—organisations that rush AI implementation without establishing trust and safe-to-speak-up norms may inadvertently increase depression and mental health risks.

Ethical leadership during AI transitions is essential; leaders must visibly model and communicate ethical principles around AI use to buffer against negative psychological outcomes, rather than treating AI adoption as a purely technical change.

Screen for depression and psychological distress during and after AI rollouts, particularly among employees who perceive low psychological safety or detect misalignment between stated values and actual AI deployment practices.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — while BCG's research likely draws on global client work, the specific sample size, methodology, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet. Applicability may vary by organisational context and industry.
takeaways: Create structured opportunities for all employees to contribute ideas without fear of embarrassment or punishment — this reduces hierarchical barriers and surfaces diverse perspectives that might otherwise go unheard.

Measure and monitor psychological safety explicitly in your team or department using validated survey measures or pulse checks, then use results to identify and address specific blockers to speaking up.
Link psychological safety initiatives to concrete outcomes relevant to your organisation (e.g. innovation, retention, error reporting) to build leadership support and sustain commitment over time.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: US-focused content from SHRM (Society for Human Resource Management); general principles of psychological safety are transferable to Australian workplaces, but specific HR policy references or US employment law citations would not apply locally.
takeaways: Identify and action the four specific leader behaviours SHRM recommends—likely including acknowledging mistakes, inviting input, and responding non-defensively to questions—then assess which your team experiences least and prioritise there.

Use a simple team survey or one-on-one check-ins to measure baseline psychological safety before implementing changes, then track whether team members increase their willingness to speak up, ask questions, or flag concerns without fear.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — sample size, geographic scope, and sector not specified in provided text. Generalisability depends on whether the study involved diverse workplaces or specific industries.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) as a foundation for employees to view AI tools as job resources rather than threats, which directly supports innovation outcomes.

Design AI implementation strategies that explicitly foster employee confidence and agency — workers with stronger psychological capital are better positioned to leverage algorithmic tools creatively rather than resist them.

Assess and strengthen your team's psychological capital before or during AI adoption; those with low baseline resilience or self-efficacy may need targeted support to reframe AI as enabling rather than constraining their work.
